title: The Road to Moscow
subtitle: Soviet defensive reorganisation and the Mozhaisk line.
author: Robert M. Dobo
summary: Zhukov rebuilds Moscow’s western defence as reports reveal fragmented survivors, redirected supplies and the limits of the Mozhaisk positions.
body:
After the rings closed

On 13 October, Georgy Zhukov had commanded the reconstructed Western Front for only three days. The armies that had protected Moscow at the beginning of the month were trapped or shattered, and the new commander had to defend the approaches with forces still being assembled. German troops were pressing through the openings created by the Vyazma disaster, but Soviet soldiers continued fighting inside the enclosure and along the routes east. The emergency was a race to establish a functioning front before the attackers could turn their breakthrough into a direct threat to the capital. Appointment to command gave Zhukov authority; the forces needed to exercise it had to be found and organised. [1]

The new defence centred on the approaches through Volokolamsk, Mozhaisk, Maloyaroslavets and Kaluga. Each corridor offered a route towards Moscow and a place where troops could attempt to block it. These sectors were related, but the strength available in one could not automatically cover another. Zhukov's command had to combine surviving formations, arriving reserves and prepared works into a line that could resist an enemy still exploiting its victory. Moscow's protection depended on the connections between those parts. A strong position could be bypassed if the neighbouring sector failed; a reserve could arrive too late if the route by which it was expected had already been cut. [1][2]

German forces had shattered much of Western and Reserve fronts and badly damaged Bryansk Front. Exploiting that breach still required an army able to move, supply itself and defeat further resistance. The mobile formations emerging beyond Vyazma carried the losses and mechanical wear of the battles that had brought them there. Soviet command reconstruction began within that interval between a broken front and a German advance that still had to be sustained.[1][3]a

A command remade in crisis

Zhukov assumed control of the combined Western and Reserve Fronts on 10 October. His appointment did not deliver a fresh army by itself. He inherited an enormous geographical responsibility at the moment when the fate of many divisions that had belonged to those fronts remained unclear. The U.S. Army's campaign history describes his assignment as manning the Mozhaisk defensive system with survivors from Vyazma, recent conscripts and seasoned troops transferred from other sectors. This was an improvised force assembled under fire. An order assigning a unit to a sector could say where it ought to stand; it did not prove that the unit had arrived with its guns, transport, signals equipment and a dependable ammunition supply.[1]

Bryansk Front’s report of 13 October shows how incomplete the picture remained. Its staff had no information from Third Army. Aircraft sent to find Eremenko and army headquarters had failed to establish contact. The report could locate parts of Fiftieth Army and describe an escape by Thirteenth Army, but it could not account for the whole front. A headquarters capable of sending a report did not necessarily know the condition or position of every army under its authority.[11][1]b

The approach sectors gave the new defence a recognisable organisation. Sixteenth Army was associated with Volokolamsk, Fifth with Mozhaisk, Forty-Third with Maloyaroslavets and Forty-Ninth with the Kaluga direction. Their assignments placed armies across the principal routes by which German forces might approach the capital. They did not create an equally strong barrier between every pair of towns. A position on the highway could be vital precisely because the neighbouring country was poorly suited to moving heavy weapons and supplies. Soviet commanders needed enough strength at these junctions to force German units to deploy for battle, while retaining the ability to reinforce another road if the enemy shifted its effort.[4][1]

The four principal approaches also divided the problem of reinforcement. Sixteenth Army could block the Volokolamsk road without thereby securing Mozhaisk; a crisis near Kaluga could threaten the southern connection while the central sector still held. Zhukov needed enough continuity to prevent another wide envelopment, but concentrating the available troops everywhere was impossible. The defence therefore relied on making the main corridors costly to penetrate while keeping reserves able to respond. The force was being organised through combat, not placed behind a completed line during a secure interval. German pressure determined how much time each sector had to prepare. [1][5][4]c

Defending the approach roads

The Mozhaisk system offered positions along threatened road corridors, with incomplete works and troops arriving at different times. On 13 October, it was still far from a continuous, fully manned barrier. Its value depended on assembling forces that could hold those approaches and support one another.[1]d

The northern and western approaches

North of the direct Smolensk–Moscow highway, Third Panzer Group pressed towards Kalinin. Its commander was now Georg-Hans Reinhardt: Hermann Hoth had been assigned to Seventeenth Army in the south on 5 October. The transfer put an experienced armoured commander in charge of a force already committed to extending the northern threat. Reaching Kalinin would expose Soviet communications and offer an approach around the western defence, but it would also pull German units away from the direct route to Moscow. On 13 October that movement was still developing; the city fell on the fourteenth. The northern danger was immediate without being a completed encirclement of the capital. [6][1]

Volokolamsk, on the northwestern approach, was one of the places in which a defence might anchor itself even if country between strongpoints remained thinly held. Farther south, Mozhaisk commanded the direct highway and railway corridor from Smolensk. These routes mattered because an army marching towards Moscow could not advance as a uniform wave through every forest and field. Tanks, heavy guns and supply trucks depended on passable roads and bridges. A railway offered large carrying capacity only after the tracks, gauge and forward unloading facilities could actually serve the force at the front. Soviet defence at a junction could therefore impose costs disproportionate to the length of trench held there. German units might go around it, but doing so demanded fuel, reconnaissance and a secure alternative route.[1][3]e

Reorganisation took place under the scrutiny of Soviet security organs. The NKVD—the People's Commissariat for Internal Affairs—used special departments and blocking detachments to detain men who had become separated from their units or fled the front. An October report from Solomon Milshtein to Lavrenty Beria, covering the war to 10 October, recorded 657,364 detained servicemen, 25,878 arrests and 10,201 executions. These were totals across fronts since the invasion, not figures for the Vyazma survivors or the Moscow battle alone. Most detained men were sent back to the front. [7]

The categories matter as much as the scale. Detention did not establish desertion, arrest did not establish guilt, and the report's labels reflected the security authorities' judgments. Edele's analysis treats these records as evidence of both military disintegration and the state's effort to recover control. The document's aggregate arithmetic is also inconsistent, so it cannot support a perfectly reconciled statistical balance. It does establish a system that combined returning soldiers to combat with imprisonment and execution. Men trying to reach Soviet lines after a defeat faced an authority that could restore them to their units or punish them as threats to discipline. [8]

Milshtein’s report separately listed 8,772 arrested men as deserters. Others were classified as spies, traitors, cowards, spreaders of provocative rumours or men who had wounded themselves. These labels are the NKVD’s, and neither the list nor its arithmetic establishes the validity of individual accusations. The document also reported 3,321 executions before assembled troops, identifying punishment performed as a warning to others. Such proceedings made the restoration of discipline visible through lethal force. The same report described returning most detained men to combat: the state sought to recover manpower while imposing exemplary penalties. Its coercion was selective rather than a uniform fate for everyone separated from a unit. [7][8]f

The same Bryansk Front report described Ermakov’s group reassembling after escape. Rifle, cavalry and tank formations survived in fragments; the 150th Tank Brigade was reported with nine tanks. These were returns for the elements then accounted for, not full establishments or a census of every survivor. Restoring a familiar formation’s name to the order of battle could not replace its missing weapons, transport, headquarters and connections with neighbouring troops.[11]g

The long southwestern corridor

The southern arm of Typhoon should not be folded into the Mozhaisk story. Guderian's Second Panzer Group, redesignated Second Panzer Army early in October, had begun its offensive two days before the main Army Group Centre attack. Its advance through Orel and towards Mtsensk threatened the approaches to Tula and, beyond that, the possibility of turning around Moscow from the south. By the thirteenth, the armoured spearhead had travelled far beyond the line at which it opened the operation, but had not already captured Tula or completed the southern encirclement of the capital.[1][3]

The route crossed country in which rivers, woods and road surfaces made speed uneven. A retrospective German terrain study stressed the difficulty of moving through the Desna basin and reaching reliable roads before wet weather. Its observations illuminate transport geography but need careful use: the study was written from German officers' experience after the war, and its emphasis on terrain can obscure the Soviet units that fought on the approaches to Mtsensk. A road did not become unusable solely because it rained; fighting, demolition, traffic congestion and the need to bring forward artillery could all stop a column. An armoured formation at its farthest point might be waiting for fuel and infantry while its leading scouts were still advancing.[9][1][3]h

The danger to Moscow from this direction was real because the city was also a rail and command hub for central Russia. German planners hoped to sever the routes by which Soviet armies could move reserves or supplies laterally. The existence of that objective did not mean it was already achieved. Tula remained a Soviet industrial and military centre; its defence would become a separate test of whether Guderian's force could convert a rapid advance to sustained movement. Soviet troops on the Mtsensk axis could delay the German column even if they could not restore the original front. The time they gained mattered only when Soviet command used it to assemble men and material along the following corridors.[1][3]

The southern danger required its own defence. Guderian's route through Orel towards Tula was part of Army Group Centre's operation, while the German armies moving on Kharkov belonged to Army Group South. The Stavka had to respond to both, but the troops protecting one industrial city could not be assumed to cover the other. This distinction became more important as the original Soviet fronts broke apart. Restoring command around Moscow meant deciding where the capital's southern protection ended and the wider southwestern front began, while maintaining connections across that boundary. The enemy's movements put those administrative divisions under immediate military pressure. [1][3]i

A city preparing while armies moved

Around Moscow, civilians were constructing defensive works. The U.S. Army history notes that the workforce was largely women, building several semicircular belts, while workers' militia battalions prepared to man positions. This labour was part of the military story, not a decorative scene behind the tanks. A ditch had to be marked, dug and tied to a defended road; an obstacle had to be placed where it would block a vehicle rather than merely look formidable on a plan. Workers used time and physical strength in a city also trying to keep transport, factories and households functioning. Whether every new work would receive trained troops and ammunition in time was uncertain.[1]

Civilian labour strengthened a defence whose field armies were short of time. The belts around Moscow added obstacles and prepared positions behind the threatened approaches. Their usefulness depended on soldiers, guns and communications arriving to make them defensible. Workers' militia formations were another effort to turn the resources of the capital into immediate military strength. Neither mobilisation abolished the effects of limited training or equipment. It nevertheless enlarged the means available to a command that had lost much of its original front. The civilians doing this work were helping to shape the conditions under which the next battle might be fought, even while the location of that battle remained uncertain. [1]j

Transport linked the city's civil and military responsibilities. Roads used by incoming formations also carried wounded people and displaced civilians east. Rail cars assigned to factories or government offices could not at the same time bring forward every military reserve. Yet an evacuation could preserve skilled workers and equipment for later production. Historians of the Soviet war economy have shown how moving industry east kept essential output possible while straining receiving regions and causing interruptions. In October, commanders could not know which removal would succeed and which would leave a factory idle for months. The immediate decision was whether a machine should continue producing near a threatened front or be disassembled before German troops could reach it.[1][5]k

A German order of 12 October gave this preparation a terrifying significance. Hitler directed that Moscow's capitulation should not be accepted and that German troops should not enter it. The order cited the danger of mines and epidemics as justifications and instructed that civilians fleeing towards German lines be driven back with fire. Movement east was welcome because it would burden and disorganise the Soviet rear; feeding the population at German expense was rejected. Artillery and air attack were to help force the city to yield without admitting its inhabitants to protection. These were instructions for a conquest Germany had not achieved. They nevertheless show that the civilian danger was part of the proposed operation itself: the leadership intended to deny a threatened population both sustenance and refuge behind German lines. [3]l

What the workers built

Much of the labour on Moscow’s defensive belts was performed by women. Digging created obstacles and strongpoints that could help the defence, but only if their siting, supporting fire and garrisons made them useful. Unfinished works or positions without troops offered limited protection.[1]m

The cost of each mile

German operational accounts often place mud at the centre of the October slowdown. Mud mattered. Snow had appeared during the pocket fighting, and successive rain and thaw made roads increasingly unreliable. But 13 October cannot be explained by saying that weather suddenly stopped an otherwise unopposed army. Soviet soldiers continued to fight in the pockets and at new roadblocks. German units needed fuel, shells, spare parts and food; vehicles that had already travelled enormous distances required maintenance. Even a dry road could not carry unlimited traffic, and a bridge damaged by combat could force a queue. Weather raised the cost of every one of these tasks; it did not create them from nothing.[1][5]

German pursuit depended on the distance between a division and the supplies that made it usable. Railway conversion could bring material into the occupied region, but the final journey still passed over roads shared by combat units, supply vehicles and the traffic returning from the front. The strain increased when formations spread towards different objectives. Fuel reaching one railhead did not resolve a shortage on another approach, and a column delayed on a road could leave the leading troops without their supporting artillery. The German command needed a concentrated blow against Moscow, yet the pursuit was dispersing its forces across an expanding and deteriorating transport network. [3][5]

Horses were equally part of this army. German infantry and artillery relied on animal transport, which needed feed, care and passable routes. A motorised spearhead could overtake the men and guns intended to hold the ground it crossed. Conversely, slow roads might allow infantry to close part of the gap, though this did not automatically restore the vehicles or their fuel stocks. The relevant question is not whether the entire German army “stopped” on 13 October. It is which formation could move, which could fight after moving, and whether a new advance could be sustained along a broad front. Different answers applied around Kalinin, Mozhaisk and Mtsensk.[1][3][5]n

Reconstruction also involved the less visible work of supply and contact. The 7 October railway instructions redirected consignments towards the emerging defence. Six days later, Bryansk Front’s report showed armies and groups still attempting to escape, regroup or reconnect with their command. Surviving men became useful fighting forces through those practical arrangements, rather than through the retention of their former unit titles alone.[11]

The defence remained under construction. Supplies needed usable destinations, and headquarters had to find formations whose last reports no longer described their situation. German delays gave Soviet commanders time, but connecting railways, surviving troops and communications was the work that turned that time into another defence.[11]o

What commanders could know

German public messaging ran ahead of the military situation. Otto Dietrich had told foreign correspondents on 9 October that the eastern campaign was decided. The German victories were large enough to give that claim an appearance of plausibility, yet his statement was propaganda made while Soviet forces still fought and while German supply and mobility problems were mounting. It is evidence of what officials wanted audiences to believe, not independent proof that the road to Moscow had become undefended. The confidence of a press briefing also affected expectations within Germany: a campaign said to be nearly won left little room in public discussion for a long winter struggle.[1]

News of the military crisis reached Moscow unevenly. On 11 October, the American ambassador Laurence Steinhardt reported that the Soviet public had received little warning until an 8 October communiqué acknowledged intense fighting around Vyazma and Bryansk. An admission concerning Orel followed. In his account, the abrupt appearance of these places in the news shocked residents accustomed to much vaguer reports of fighting along the front. This was the ambassador's observation of the information climate, not a survey of the city's population. It nonetheless helps explain why preparations for evacuation could provoke such alarm a few days later: the public had to absorb a sudden change in the apparent proximity and seriousness of the German threat.[10][1]p

The German breakthrough had created a dangerous opportunity while leaving Soviet forces still fighting or emerging from enclosure. Fresh formations entered the approaches as headquarters tried to locate survivors and redirect supplies. The contest now depended on which side could combine its remaining resources into effective action sooner. October’s enclosures had transformed that struggle without deciding it.[2][1]

The Soviet position remained precarious at the end of 13 October. Zhukov had restored a command framework and concentrated attention on the main approaches, but he had not removed the threat from the north or the pressure on the western corridors. Kalinin's loss on the following day would deepen the crisis, and emergency decisions in Moscow would follow. Those developments were still ahead. The immediate achievement was more limited: German forces advancing beyond the October pockets were encountering another defence, assembled from survivors, reserves and the labour of the threatened capital. Its existence gave Moscow a chance to continue resisting; its strength would be tested at once. [1]

On 13 October, the road to Moscow was being contested through the rebuilding of Soviet forces and the effort to sustain German pursuit. The defence still had plain weaknesses. In Crisis at the Capital, that military danger reaches the government offices, workplaces and streets of Moscow itself.[1]q
